title: MoodleMoot Europe Conference Notes 2026
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill reports from MoodleMoot Europe in Barcelona and argues that the most important developments were a leadership change and a strategic framing, not a product launch. Martin Dougiamas has left Moodle HQ to pursue independent research on AI and the future of education, a consequential shift that Hill says received little attention. New CEO Scott Anderberg's keynote on sovereignty, built around the question 'Who gets to decide?', gives Moodle a way to speak to institutions that care about control over software, delivery, and data without caring about open source history. Hill credits the core product improvements but is concerned that the academic product vision, including the Moodle Higher Ed idea, has stalled. He frames Moodle as caught in a '100 Million Learner Paradox', with huge registration numbers but difficulty winning or keeping institutions, as shown by UNSW moving to D2L Brightspace. He also notes that Moodle's AI roadmap stays optional and integration-based, and that the certified integrations program shows HQ making firmer choices. His conclusion is that the sovereignty framing could be a lynchpin, but HQ still has to decide what it means for the academic product.
points: Martin Dougiamas has left Moodle HQ and now pursues his AI and education research independently, which raises the question of who inside the company connects that experimentation to the product roadmap.

Anderberg's three sovereignty questions (rights to the software, how it is delivered, and where data is held) are most useful because they add the ability to change those decisions later, including swapping AI models or providers.
Hill warns that Europe risks 'GDPR-ing' the idea of sovereignty by confusing writing policies with actually achieving independence.
Moodle's 500 million registered users mask weak adoption among universities, and the UNSW move to D2L Brightspace shows the installed base can leave.
Certified integrations and the plugin marketplace show HQ making firmer ecosystem choices, but tighter vendor relationships also increase platform influence over how tools reach customers.
quotes: Sovereignty was everywhere at this conference. In quite a few conversations, it sounded like a new label for the open source arguments of the 2000s.

Scott's keynote went further. He traced how sovereignty evolved from the authority of monarchs to states, communities, and individuals, then brought the discussion down to a question people could use:
An institution might choose a managed service today and another provider later. It might use one AI model and replace it when capabilities, costs, or terms change.

Europe wants to avoid being beholden to American Big Tech companies, but it also loves policies and regulations über alles. Think of GDPR: cookie approvals that no one reads, horrible website experiences, and burdensome compliance for startups.
Her argument was that AI makes producing a course easier, but does not ensure that it is a good course. Moodle should help educators design for learning, with better alignment and assessment.
Moodle boasts over 500 million registered users, yet I continue to hear from institutions and partners about the difficulty of getting universities and training providers to adopt it.

AI will remain optional and delivered through integrations in Moodle LMS, while Workplace could incorporate more native functionality. Some Moodle installations operate with unreliable electricity and connectivity; requiring AI for core teaching and learning would undermine those uses.
These moves can make third-party tools easier to adopt while increasing the platform company's influence over how they reach customers.
